info_tile.heading: What is MVPF?
info_tile.description: The Marginal Value of Public Funds (MVPF) is a metric that measures the social welfare benefit of a policy per dollar of government spending. It represents how much value beneficiaries receive relative to what the policy costs.
info_tile.formula: Most MVPF work looks at policies where the person subject to the policy is also the main beneficiary, such as cash transfers. Detention is different. Jail is imposed on detainees but is justified as benefiting the general public. That is why this tool tracks both Detainee effects and broader Society effects when calculating the MVPF of detention.
info_tile.application_label: Our application of MVPF to Cook County Jail
info_tile.application: In most MVPF work, people plug in causal estimates for how behavior changes at the intensive margin (for example, working a bit more or less when a benefit changes). For Cook County Jail, we do not have credible intensive-margin estimates for detention, and the policy questions we are interested in are about the extensive margin and the scale of the jail itself: who is detained at all, for how long, and what level of funding or even continued operation is justified. It uses the full annual costs of operating the jail and the full set of impacts on people who are detained to summarize those tradeoffs in an MVPF-style framework. This CCJ calculator is built to help you see how assumptions about extensive-margin harms and benefits feed into both the numerator and the denominator, using 2018 jail spending as the benchmark. For a fuller discussion of this choice and its limits, see the longer explanation [link to MVPF Explained].

applying_to_detention.heading: Applying MVPF to detention in Cook County Jail
applying_to_detention.paragraph1: Most MVPF work looks at policies where the person subject to the policy is also the main beneficiary, such as cash transfers. Detention is different. Jail is imposed on detainees but is justified as benefiting the general public. That is why this tool tracks both Detainee effects and broader Society effects when calculating the MVPF of detention.
applying_to_detention.paragraph2: Most studies on detention focus on marginal changes, like one extra day in jail or one additional person detained. This tool instead looks at the overall or infra-marginal picture for a facility, using Cook County Jail as the baseline case. It uses the full annual costs of operating the jail and the full set of impacts on people who are detained to summarize those tradeoffs in an MVPF-style framework.

detainee_values.title: Detainee Values
detainee_values.description: Detainee Values capture the total harm detention imposes on people who are jailed. We measure this using a willingness-to-pay lens, estimating how much a person would trade to avoid being detained. This reflects short-term harms, disruptions to work and family life, and long-term effects on health, income, and stability.

harm_valuation.button_text: Willingness to Pay derived from Relative Harm Valuation
harm_valuation.explanation: The baseline detainee component, which measures harm by comparing each day in custody to crime-victimization cost benchmarks such as robbery or aggravated assault. This produces a larger per-day harm value than detainee self-reported WTP (~$4,000/day), and scales with whatever length of stay (non-linearly), population, or charge mix the user chooses. Because it reflects broader social harm rather than ability-to-pay limits, it is used as the default. Source: crime-harm equivalence estimates from Stevenson & Mayson (2022).

wtp_freedom.explanation: An alternative detainee valuation based on stated willingness-to-pay (WTP) per day to avoid jail, drawn from surveys of people facing detention. Valued at $11/day in 2018 dollars. This approach reflects detainees' own monetary tradeoffs and can be scaled using any assumed length of stay or detainee population. It typically produces much smaller harm estimates than the baseline Relative Harm Valuation, which makes the overall MVPF less negative and is therefore a more conservative choice. Source: detainee WTP evidence summarized in Stevenson & Mayson (2022).

society_values.title: Society Values
society_values.description: Society Values measure how detention affects external factors like public safety, victimization risk, and community wellbeing. These values summarize the effects felt by people outside the jail and convert those effects into a common dollar scale for comparison.

crime_prevention.explanation: This component captures any crime-prevention benefit from incapacitation during detention. In the baseline model, this is set to zero in line with empirical evidence suggesting minimal net crime reduction from pretrial detention. Users can adjust this assumption in alternative scenarios.

court_appearance.explanation: Included as a baseline society component because court appearance is a central justification for pretrial detention. This component places a dollar value on avoiding failures to appear (FTA) by combining administrative costs of warrant issuance and possible rearrest with an assumed FTA probability. Source: Fishbane, Ouss & Shah (2020) and Cook County court data.

community_spillovers.explanation: This component captures broader community effects of detention, including impacts on families, neighborhoods, and local economies. Effects include lost wages, disrupted caregiving, and reduced community stability. These spillovers extend the costs of detention beyond the individual detainee.

government_cost.title: Government Cost
government_cost.description: Government Cost reflects all public spending required to run the detention system. This includes daily operations, staffing, healthcare, facilities, court processing, and administrative overhead. It represents the fiscal cost taxpayers bear to support the current level of detention.

operational.explanation: The baseline government cost component, representing the full operating budgets for the Cook County Department of Corrections and Cermak Health Services. These expenses include staffing, food, medical care, housing, and other daily operations, and they can be allocated over any assumed detainee count or length of stay. Since these costs reflect actual fiscal outlays, they form the default denominator of the MVPF. Source: Cook County FY2018 Appropriation Budget.

crime_increase.button_text: Costs associated with Crime Effect: Increase
crime_increase.explanation: Government costs that arise if detention leads to increased crime post-release (criminogenic effect). This includes additional law enforcement, court processing, victim services, and potential future incarceration costs. Evidence suggests detention can increase recidivism for some populations.

crime_decrease.button_text: Costs associated with Crime Effect: Decrease
crime_decrease.explanation: Government savings that occur if detention prevents crimes through incapacitation or deterrence. This includes avoided law enforcement costs, reduced court processing, and lower victim compensation. The magnitude depends on assumptions about detention's crime-prevention effectiveness.

overview_intro.title: Overview Tab Introduction
overview_intro.paragraph1: This dashboard lets you explore how different assumptions change the Marginal Value of Public Funds (MVPF) for pretrial detention in Cook County Jail. The MVPF compares the total harms and benefits created by detention to the public cost of operating the jail. You can adjust several inputs that determine the number of people detained, the composition of cases, and the avergae length of stay. These inputs reshape the numerator and denominator of the MVPF and let you test how sensitive the results are to policy or system changes.
overview_intro.paragraph2:
Each scenario shows an MVPF for pretrial detention that compares harms and benefits to the public cost of running Cook County Jail in 2018. In every scenario, the numerator is built from two types of components: 
 • harms to detainees, valued in dollars per day in custody 
 • effects on society, such as changes in court appearance or crime outcomes
overview_intro.paragraph3: The denominator is always the 2018 operating cost of the jail, scaled by the population and length of stay choices you set above, plus any costs or savings associated with crime outcomes.
overview_intro.paragraph4: The scenarios below offer three different normative stances on how to value detention. They differ only in how detainee harm is measured and whether spillover harms to the detainee’s community are included. By default, the crime effect parameter is set to zero in every scenario. If you turn on a nonzero crime effect, it will change both the numerator (through assumed social costs or benefits of crime) and the denominator (through changes in government spending on policing, courts, and incarceration). Use these scenarios and parameters to see how alternative value judgments and crime assumptions shift the MVPF and what that implies about the social return of pretrial detention under different assumptions.

mvpf_purpose.title: How the MVPF for Cook County Jail was calculated?
mvpf_purpose.content: This section will explain the purpose and methodology of the MVPF calculation, including how the baseline values are derived and what they represent in the context of Cook County Jail operations.

scenarios_explanation.title: Placeholder for Alternative Scenarios Description
scenarios_explanation.content: Explanation of the different scenarios available (baseline, conservative, reduced crime, etc.) and how they differ from each other in terms of assumptions and parameters.

scenario_intro_p1: The three scenarios differ only in how we value harm to detainees (a larger Relative Harm Valuation scale versus a smaller survey-based "Willingness to Pay for Freedom") and whether we add an extra negative term for spillover harms to the detainee’s community. In all scenarios, the crime effect components are set to zero by default; they only change if you adjust that parameter elsewhere in the dashboard.
